inline.s: [The four views, which are not the four views] The Diamond Sutra
original text:

“World-Honored One, the views of self, the views of persons, the views of sentient beings, and the views of a lifespan are not the views of self, the views of persons, the views of sentient beings, and the views of a lifespan; thus they are called the views of self, the views of persons, the views of sentient beings, and the views of a lifespan.”
(For the commentary, see
The Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
But these wicked monks did not give up, and lodged a complaint with the censorial office. The censorial office accepted their complaint and ordered the criminal tribunal
(the officials in charge of criminal matters)
to hear the case.

When the notice came down, the Master drifted out of the mountain and went to the censorial office to await the hearing. He lodged on a boat on the Lotus River, and waited a whole year without the case being tried, and the money he had on him ran out. At this time the assistant prefect Xiang Chudong, who was living at home on the Han
hán

River, invited the Master to come. The Master took a boat and set out, but on the way met a great wind; the boat broke and sank in the river, and the Master was rescued. Having with difficulty reached Sir Xiang's home, he once more fell gravely ill and nearly died, and Sir Xiang summoned physicians who did their utmost to save him. By the time he returned to the prefectural seat, he was lying ill awaiting the trial.
In the thirty-eighth year of the Wanli era
the Master
was sixty-five. This year he still lived on the boat awaiting the trial. In the seventh month of autumn, the Imperial Commissioner
(the official specially appointed to inspect and handle affairs of local government)

made his inspection tour and came to the prefecture to call upon the Master. When the officials hearing the case learned of this, they knew the case could be delayed no longer and could only begin the trial. The result of the trial was that the accusation was judged to be true, and the Master was found guilty of a transgression and was to be escorted out of the jurisdiction.

When the Imperial Commissioner learned of this, he strongly disapproved and rebutted, saying, “Master Hanshan has done great service for the Sixth Patriarch; all the work was personally planned by the Master, and all the funds were personally raised by the Master. Now the wicked monks have profited, and instead the Master is sentenced as guilty. Is this the gate of equality?” Thereupon he ordered the local circuit
(the local circuit and prefecture)
to investigate the case strictly. The circuit and prefecture
(the administrative head of the circuit-level local government)

at once set out, going in person into the Caoxi mountains, and examined the accusation of the wicked monks item by item. The result of the examination confirmed that the wicked monks had falsely accused the Master of misappropriating more than eight thousand taels of the monastery's funds, and that it was all a lie.

At the beginning, when the Master established the rules of the monastery storehouse office, he instituted numbered tickets. All receipts and disbursements of money and grain were recorded in writing by the overseers, and every sum received or spent had a numbered ticket as its voucher. At this time, the monks who had served in past years, relying on the numbered tickets, audited and calculated before the circuit and prefecture. The result was that the Master was untainted by a hair's worth. Only then did all, high and low, within and without, believe the Master was pure and without flaw, and the matter of the false accusation became clear to the whole world. The circuit and prefecture were furious and wished to deal severely with the wicked monks; had it not been for the Master's intercession, they could hardly have escaped with their lives.

Seeing the Master was so noble and pure, the circuit and prefecture urged him again and again to stay in the mountain, but the Master was already weary of it and declined with all his might. He handed over the meditation hall to his disciple Huaiyu, and drifted away for good. At the earnest request of the disciples at Wuyang, he took up residence at the Changchun Hermitage in Wuyang.
When the Master left Caoxi, he composed ten quatrains to give to his disciples, of which the following three are recorded:
The seed of merit's field must be planted deep, / Cause and effect as on a bright mirror's face. / A thousand times you've come to the treasure-mount; / This time you must not go back empty again.

Labor with diligence, no fear of toil, / Think of the stone once hung about the waist. / When one breath fails, ten thousand aeons pass; / Without planting virtue's root the suffering's hard to erase.
[The stone once hung about the waist] The Sixth Patriarch once hung a stone about his waist while husking rice. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“The Patriarch
(the Fifth Patriarch)
secretly went to the husking shed, and seeing Huineng
(Huineng)
husking rice with a stone about his waist, said, “One who seeks the Way should forget the body for the Dharma; is this not so?””

[Husking rice with a stone about the waist] In ancient times, when husking a great quantity of rice, the principle of the lever was used, with the pestle on one end and a person treading on the other. Huineng tied a great stone about his waist to add weight to his body, so that the counterweight on the opposite side, at the pestle, could be heavier, thereby increasing the efficiency of husking the rice.
Do not let a lifetime pass lightly by, / Time flies like an arrow, a thing to startle. / Only fear that when the breath fails so soon, / When will you come again to the treasure-mount?
When the Master went to the southern mountain, he left ten quatrains for his disciples of Lingnan, of which the following three are recorded:
The matter is clear before your very self, / Do not go outward asking of fortune and fate. / But turn back the light where'er you touch, / And let no worldly toil entangle the true master.

[This matter] This affair. [Before your very self] Practicing it yourself (carrying it out personally). [Worldly toil] The labor of the mind in the dusty realms; another name for affliction. [The true master] The master of the house, meaning one's intrinsic nature.

The great Way never was apart from the true root, / Most often division makes near kin and far. / You must see through the face born of your mother, / Only then are you one who truly discerns amid the dust.
For the Dharma, who would shrink from the long road
(the endless distance)
, / How can one call the miasmic sea the very end of the sky? / Let but a single drop of the water of Caoxi / Water the flower of five leaves come from the West
(the coming of the patriarch Bodhidharma from the West)

[The flower of five leaves] After the Sixth Patriarch Huineng, the Chan school branched into the five schools of Caodong, Linji, Yunmen, Weiyang, and Fayan, and so is called one flower with five leaves.
In the thirty-ninth year of the Wanli era (

), the Master was sixty-six. The Master was recuperating from illness at Dinghu Mountain in Duanzhou. There were many Confucian scholars who came to seek his instruction, and the Master wrote a Resolving Doubts on the Great Learning.

The next year the Master moved to the Changchun Hermitage at Wuyang, where he explained to his disciples the Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana, the Verse on the Eight Consciousnesses, the Treatise on the Gateway of the Hundred Dharmas, and others. And because his Staccato Notes on the Lotus Sutra were so interconnected in meaning and structure that scholars could hardly grasp them, he also wrote the Sectional Notes on the Lotus Sutra.
In the fortieth year of the Wanli era (

), the Master was sixty-seven. The Master held the summer retreat at the Changchun Hermitage and explained the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment to his disciples. The exposition had barely reached half when suddenly a severe back abscess broke out, as large as a rice bowl; the several physicians who were called could not cure it, and his life hung by a thread. The great general of Wuyang was preparing to arrange the Master's last affairs. Just then a local physician named Liang Xingshan arrived, as if summoned by a spirit. As soon as he saw the Master's back abscess he said, “This is a beehive abscess, already very dangerous; if delayed any longer it will be beyond saving!” He at once went up the mountain to gather herbs, pounded and applied them, and there was an immediate effect; by winter he had completely recovered. After the abscess healed, the Master wrote an article to thank
(see
the Dream-Wander Collection, Preface Presented to the Good Physician Liang Xingshan

. The abscess the Master now had was the same as when he first learned to sit in meditation forty-eight years earlier, both being karmic debts from past lives. Though it had often broken out during these forty-eight years, it had always stopped after prayer, and this time was to be the final repayment of that karmic debt.

[Summer retreat] Also called abiding, meaning that during the three months of summer the monks may not go out at will, in order to devote themselves to sitting in meditation and cultivating the Dharma.
The next year

, the Master left the Changchun Hermitage for Hengyang, where he gave the precepts to the monks at the Great Virtue Monastery. The layman Feng Yuancheng built the Tanhua Hermitage for the Master, as a place for spreading the Dharma. At this time the Empress Dowager passed away, and the Master established a repaying-kindness bodhimanda here, and, facing the tablet of the Empress Dowager, shaved his head, gave thanks for the imperial favor, and put on the monk's robe again.
[Putting on the monk's robe again] The Master's monastic status was restored in
, and it was not until

, when the Empress Dowager passed away and he built the repaying-kindness bodhimanda, that he faced the tablet of the Empress Dowager, shaved his head, gave thanks for the imperial favor, and put on the monk's robe again. The depth of his gratitude is beyond words.

When the Master was at the Eastern Sea he had resolved to write a General Discussion of the Surangama, but because he had no leisure he had not begun it. In the fifth month of this year he set to work, and in fifty days the draft was finished. Just then his accomplished disciples Wuxin and Zhuanyu came to visit, and the Master composed verses to give them:
The verse Sending the Abbot Wuxinrong Back to Jingkou says:
In the empty mountain I thought to keep me to the end of years, / Who would have thought you'd go east and board the Dharma-boat?
Wait till above the sea gate the lonely moon arises, / And for this old monk round off the tale of the word.
The verse Asking After the Illness of Zhuanyu Heng says:
The four greats have long been seen as bubbles and shadows; / Where can the demon of illness find a place to hide?
The ancients had their own method of serene ease, / It lies only in the single thought of the unborn.
In the forty-third year of the Wanli era (

), the Master was seventy. In the spring of this year the Master explained the General Discussion of the Surangama to the assembly. In the fourth month the Master composed the General Discussion of the Lotus Sutra, because neither the Staccato Notes nor the Sectional Notes on the Lotus Sutra had fully threaded together the whole text; so he wrote this general discussion to make up for their omissions. Then the Master went on to explain the Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana and to write the Annotated Summary of the Awakening of Faith.

The next year was the twelfth anniversary of Master Daguan's death, and the Master could not forget the bond of their friendship in the Dharma and had long wished to go in person to mourn him. In the fourth month the Master left Hudong, and at the Dragon Boat Festival came to Wuchang to pay homage to the great Buddha. He visited Mount Jiufeng and paid homage to the pagoda of Chan Master Wunian. In the sixth month he reached Xunyang, visited the Donglin Monastery, and wrote poems of remembrance of antiquity. He climbed Mount Lu to pay homage to the pagoda of Chan Master Chekong. In summer he sought relief from the heat at Jinzhu Ping, where he wrote the Commentary on the Zhao Treatise. The secluded beauty of Mount Lu made the Master wish to retire here. So he toured all the scenic spots of the mountain, spreading the Dharma with conditions along the way. In the seventh month he visited the Guizong Monastery
(located at the foot of Mount Lu in Jiangxi)
, climbed Golden Wheel Peak, paid homage to the relic pagoda, and left some poems here as well.
At this time a monk made a gift to the Master of the Wuru Temple
(located below the Wuru Peak south of Mount Lu)
, and the Master, seeing that it was very secluded and quiet, was quite pleased; later the disciples built a hermitage there.
In the eighth month the Master went to Huangmei
(today's Huangmei County in Hubei Province)

to pay homage to the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin and the Fifth Patriarch Hongren of the Chan school. He entered Purple Cloud Mountain, passed through Tongcheng, visited Mount Fu, climbed Mount Jiuhua, reached Jinsha, crossed Liang Creek, reached Mount Hui, passed through Wujiang, and all along the way met old friends and spoke of the Dharma, until at last he arrived at the Jizhao Hermitage on Mount Jing.

At Mount Jing, together with many of Master Daguan's disciples, the Master commemorated Master Daguan. The Master wrote a memorial, set it alight in cremation, and then placed Master Daguan's relics on Manjusri Terrace. His disciple Fakai built a pagoda, and the Master composed a pagoda inscription to be engraved before it.

That year the Master spent the New Year at Mount Jing, and opened the hall to expound the Essentials of Investigating Chan to the assembly. Because Fakai asked about the meaning of the Dharma-characteristic school, the Master wrote a Treatise on Worldly Characteristics. Around this time the Master also wrote a Song of the Plank-Carrying Fellow, together with its preface, which is quoted below:

The Dharma cave of Mount Jing, ever since Dahui revived the way of Linji, has continued the life of wisdom, and in each generation there have been those to carry it on. In recent times the Chan gate has fallen silent, its echo long gone. Lately, a throng of those practicing investigation has filled the mountain. Among them there are even some who, in a single glimpse
(seeing their nature)

, have had the reality appear before them and attained great freedom. What a pity they sit on the pure ground and will not let it go, taking it as something extraordinary, not knowing it has instead become a hindrance to the Dharma; in the teaching it is called the obstacle of what is known. Therefore the ancients said: “Even if you have done
(supposing you did so)

‘the bright moon in the cold pool, the bell in the still night, responding to the striker without loss, touching the waves without scattering’, this is still an affair on the shore of birth and death.” That is to say, it is easy to set foot among the brambles, but hard to turn your body beneath the moonlit curtain. People cling to the pole-top, still and sunk in dead water. Even this is not permitted to them, let alone those who, having not yet glimpsed, have casually attained a flash of lightning samadhi and take it as attainment, playing with the shadow of consciousness. This is taking a little as enough in the practice of Chan, the common sickness of all ages. Fearing it may fall into worldly discourse and mislead many, when someone asked for instruction, he laughingly wrote the Song of the Plank-Carrying Fellow to show him.
